newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Greater Romania likely to remain a dream.
newsitem.headline: Greater Romania likely to remain a dream.

text.p: President Emil Constantinescu led Romanians on Sunday in celebrating the creation of Greater Romania 78 years ago, but the concept will almost certainly remain a shortlived dream in modern Europe.
Constantinescu attended a religious service led by heads of the Romanian Orthodox Church in the cathedral of Alba Iulia where Ferdinand 1 was crowned "King of all Romanians" in 1922.

Greater Romania, which incorporated parts of what are now Moldova, Ukraine and Bulgaria, existed for 22 years until it was destroyed by a carve-up of the region plotted by Nazi Germany and Soviet dictator Josef Stalin.
Historians say greater Romania was born at Alba Iulia on December 1, 1918, when Transylvania, previously a part of the Austro-Hungarian empire, joined the old Kingdom of Romania.
Some 100,000 Romanians cheered political leaders on that day in the city built by the Romans, 400 km (250 miles) northwest of Bucharest.

"It was a coronation. Months after Bessarabia and Bucovina joined the country, Transylvania also joined," historian Ioan Chiper said in an interview. "More than half Romania's population lived there."
Greater Romania, like Poland, Finland, the former Czechoslovakia and ex-Yugoslavia, was born after the collapse of the Russian and Austro-Hungarian empires during World War One.
King Ferdinand I was crowned in Alba Iulia four years after Romania's unification in 1918 had been approved under post-war peace treaties.
The dream did not last long.

In 1940, the northeast heartlands of Bessarabia and Bucovina, part of Russia and Austria-Hungary before World War One, were again lost -- this time to Moscow under secret protocols of a Nazi-Soviet pact.
Most of Bessarabia is in present-day Moldova, where 60 percent of the population is ethnic Romanian. Ukraine holds the rest, along with northern Bucovina.
With the Nazis controlling nearly all of Europe, Hitler decided that same year to give northwest Transylvania to Hungary and a small slice of territory to Bulgaria.

Transylvania reverted to Romania after the war but lands handed to the Soviet Union remained in Kremlin hands. Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu frequently defied the Soviet line in foreign policy, but never openly sought their return.
Nationalists were elated by the 1991 collapse of Soviet rule and for a short time pressed for unification with Moldova.
The wave rapidly fizzled out. The vocal Greater Romania Party (PRM) got no more than five percent in November's parliamentary polls, the third post-communist vote in Romania.
Closer ties with Romania are an issue in second round presidential elections in Moldova on Sunday, pitting incumbent Mircea Snegur against the leftist speaker of parliament.

Sunday's festivities, two days after Constantinescu was sworn in as president, mark the end of another cycle for Romania -- the break with its communist past after centrists defeated ex-communists in general elections last month.
Apart from religious services, military parades were held and politicians who championed Romanian union laid wreaths at public statues.
Constantinescu was to leave later for a summit in Portugal of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe -- the start of a mission to secure NATO and European Union membership.
"While outlining the need for moral reparations for the wrongs done to Romania, the focus of our foreign policy remains integration into NATO and the European Union," Harnagea said.
